title: Trump administration reportedly plans to end Medicare subsidy that tempers drug costs for seniors – live
summary: The change will stop $3.6bn in subsidies, making the cost of prescription drug plans more expensive for seniors next year, the Wall Street Journal reports
body: The Senate is now debating the nomination of Jay Clayton, the current US attorney for the southern district of New York, as the US director of national intelligence. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, spoke in opposition to the nomination, calling Clayton an unqualified conspiracy theorist. “He has repeated baseless conspiracy theories about American elections, refused to acknowledge who won the 2020 election and participated in an abusive investigation of American journalists while providing false testimony to Congress about that investigation,” Wyden said. “It has been clear for months that under this administration, the main qualification to be DNI is the willingness to use the position to spread conspiracy theories about elections and to help Donald Trump make it harder for Americans to vote",” Wyden continued. “Even before his nomination, Mr. Clayton decided he’d show how eager he is to serve as Trump’s election conspiracy wing man,” the senator added. “I was especially alarmed by his conspiracy mongering about vote by mail. That’s how my home state of Oregon has been voting successfully for years.” “The first two senators elected by mail were a Democrat and a Republican. Vote by mail benefits rural voters who live far away from polling stations. Vote by mail benefits older people who may not be able to drive. It’s never been partisan, certainly not until Donald Trump, aided by people like Jay Clayton, made it a part of the attack on American democracy,” Wyden said. The senator also criticized Clayton for his “role in the abuse of subpoenas issued to the journalists at the New York Times”. Donald Trump is pushing the longtime vaccine opponent and current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr to be more aggressive on cutting vaccines in the US, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal. Trump has a long record of anti-vaccine statements, but the White House recently put a hold on vaccine changes after polling indicated they were a losing issue in the midterm elections. Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services, recently slashed the routine childhood immunization schedule in an unprecedented move. Trump reportedly asked Kennedy at his northern Virginia golf course in May if the health secretary had the “yips”, according to the Journal. Trump wasn’t talking about a sudden inability to make putts. Kennedy wasn’t making enough cuts to the US vaccination schedule, Trump reportedly said. The US president hopes to make “alleviating autism” a component of his legacy, the Journal reported – and he has taken issue with Kennedy’s less aggressive changes to vaccination recommendations in recent months. “Donald Trump has been anti-vaccine at least since 2015,” said Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center and an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. At the Republican primary debate that year, Trump said that autism had gotten “totally out of control” and vaccines should be in “smaller doses over a longer period of time”. Trump regularly posted on social media about debunked links between vaccination and autism as early as 2014, and his posts on Truth Social have recently advocated for breaking up shots into individual components and delaying some childhood vaccines for more than a decade. The Trump administration plans to stop paying subsidies to health insurance companies that helped to lower premiums for Medicare drug plans, the Wall Street Journal reports. The change will stop the estimated $3.6bn in subsidies that went to insurance companies this year, making the cost of prescription drug plans, known as Part D, more expensive for seniors starting next year, according to administration officials. About 25 million Americans have Part D plans, but the change will not take effect until after the upcoming midterm elections. Elsewhere today, Democratic mayors from around the country have convened in Atlanta for a quiet conversation about managing cities amid the provocations of the Trump Admniistration. The theme for the conference is “Mayors Deliver”, with discussion about housing, public safety, affordability, jobs and other Democratic touchstones. DNC chair Ken Martin, under fire and managing internecine conflict within the party, was on the panel of speakers opening the event this morning, as was former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms - the Democratic nominee in the Georgia governor’s race - and Atlanta’s current mayor Andre Dickens. Industry groups, including those from the surveillance camera, artificial intelligence and data center sectors, feature on the discussion calendar. Attendees will also be discussing election security and voter turnout. Quentin Lucas, mayor of Kansas City and president of the Democratic Mayor Association, described the fraught relationship his city’s political establishment has with Republican state and federal leaders. Republicans feel it necessary to signal their fidelity to the president and his agenda with increasingly harsh attacks on Democratic-led city governments, he said. “It’s the problem of modern politics,” the progressive mayor said of Mike Kehoe, Missouri’s conservative Republican governor. “He’s a good Christian man. I believe I am too, so we have perfectly fine conversations. In Donald Trump’s America, you can sit with somebody and share things and talk about family and all of that. But when you ask, ‘Hey, can I get a common-sense, moderate appointed to this board? Can we protect a congressional district in a state with only two Black congresspeople and two Democratic seats?’ The answer is often, ‘I gotta do what I gotta do.’ And I think that to me is probably the greatest challenge.” Lucas is facing a federal lawsuit initiated by Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, a Republican. The 22 July filing alleges that the city’s Minority and Women Business Enterprise contracting program unlawfully uses race and sex in awarding public contracts and violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Missouri man at the center of the suit has a decades-old federal fraud conviction, which the attorney general’s office ignored before filing suit. Lucas likened the suit to the president drawing city names at random out of a hat to attack. He described the suit as yet another attack on Democratic governance facilitated by the erosion of longstanding legal norms under Trump. I’ve been thinking this for years. Trump is the accelerant for all of it. The goal is to have no Black people in power, no Black people in the upper reaches of business. And its odd, because Trump was the first Republican presidential candidate who actually could get some minority numbers. But they are so - in some ways - uncomfortable with fighting it out for real, trying to persuade people of different backgrounds, which is something me and Andre [Dickens of Atlanta], and every mayor of an American city - except for the really, really Black ones - have had to do. Sean Hannity also addressed Benjamin Netanyahu, saying that Lindsey Graham “loved you, he loved the state of Israel, he loved the people of Israel”. He said Graham was Israel’s strongest ally in the Senate and “would have been blown away” that Netanyahu came to his funeral. Sean Hannity went on to recognize Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who is also in attendance at Lindsey Graham’s funeral. Hannity said: “President Zelenskyy, I know that Lindsey would have been deeply moved and honored that you made this long journey to be here today.” He added: “In our private conversations, he often marveled at your strength against the world, one of the world’s most brutal regimes. He saw you, as he said it to me once, as a warrior poet or a warrior comedian, to use those terms, and on paper, I think everybody would agree.” Eulogizing Lindsey Graham, Fox News host Sean Hannity said the South Carolina senator was “great for ratings because people listened to him.” “He drew you in, he had that passion to draw you in so far that, I was very grateful” Hannity said. He also acknowledged Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s presence in the cathedral, saying: “Lindsey would have been blown away that you took this long journey…to be here today.” Reflecting on Graham’s staunch support for Israel, Hannity said: “Just as president Trump has been Israel’s strongest friend in the history of the White House… Lindsey was that friend to Israel in the United States senate as long as I’ve known this man.” Donald Trump has ended his eulogy for Lindsey Graham, calling the late senator “strong and steadfast.” “As a brother, a senator, a warrior, and a patriot, he withstood every last test, every single test that you can go through in every trial… Lindsey, we love you. God bless you,” Trump said. Donald Trump, who ran against Lindsey Graham in the 2016 presidential election, said that “Lindsey and I did not exactly get off to the best of starts.” Recalling his leaking of Graham’s phone number to the public after Graham called him a “jackass” during the presidential race, Trump said: "It was Lindsey who had the last laugh because while I blew up his phone all for one day, we became great friends, and Lindsey did not stop calling me for the next 10 years. It was not easy.” Donald Trump said Lindsey Graham was “extremely hawkish,” adding: “I will tell you, he never saw a war that he didn’t like. Only his true friends would understand that. But he wanted it for the good of our country.” Throughout his career, Graham supported the US’s involvement in multiple wars, including its invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan, as well as the US support for Ukraine in its war against Russia, and the US’s latest war against Iran. Donald Trump went off script for a brief moment, calling Lindsey Graham “a tough cookie.” “But no matter how heated things got in Washington, virtually everyone, Republican or Democrat, liked Lindsey. Well, not everybody, but it sounds good. Not everybody,”…

title: Japan earthquake injures at least 100 and kills two inside shopping mall
summary: Kumamoto shaken by 6.8-magnitude quake, knocking out power and damaging buildings, as people remain trapped inside shopping centre
body: A 6.8-magnitude earthquake has shaken south Japan, killing at least two people and leaving at least 100 people injured. Some are trapped and presumed dead inside a shopping mall. The earthquake hit Kumamoto prefecture on the southern Kyushu island late on Tuesday afternoon, knocking out power to thousands of homes and damaging roads, bridges and buildings. The prefectural government said rescuers working at the scene overnight had taken eight people out of the Aeon Mall Kumamoto shopping centre. Of those eight, two women in their 20s were confirmed dead, while one other person was reported to be in cardiopulmonary arrest. The ⁠five others were injured but officials said their condition was not life-threatening. Firefighters said earlier that an explosion had occurred in the mall shortly after the earthquake, with a government official telling reporters that a gas leak had been reported but the cause was not known. Footage showed one side of the mall, the prefecture’s largest with roughly 200 shops, was torn away, exposing steel beams ‌and leaving debris strewn across the neighbouring car park. Several ambulances and fire engines were parked outside as rescue teams searched for survivors. Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, told reporters authorities were still assessing the extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by another deadly quake a decade ago. “We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” Takaichi said. “I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.” About 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said. The areas with the biggest tremors will remain at risk of further strong quakes and landslides for about a week since the shallow earthquake is triggering seismic activity in the area, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA). So far there have been more than 60 aftershocks ranging in magnitude from 1 to 4, the agency said. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after the quake, but was lifted within two hours. One person was killed in south-west Japan when a house collapsed during the earthquake, Kyodo News reported. Two hospitals reported more than 50 injuries each, including 10 in a serious condition, the public broadcaster NHK said. “People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people,” NHK quoted one hospital employee as saying. “Inside the hospital, there are water leaks and electrical system failures.” Several people on a high-speed ‌train at the time of the quake were also ‌injured and more were missing after a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, according to local media reports. Takaichi pledged late yesterday that emergency responders would work “tirelessly” through the night “starting with the rescue and lifesaving of those affected”. Footage from NHK showed several other buildings on fire or partly collapsed, along with large fissures on ‌major roads, including an elevated highway. TSMC, the world’s largest contract chip maker, Sony and Fujifilm evacuated workers from their factories in the area. Chiharu Hara, a 35-year-old recruitment agent who was in Kumamoto, told AFP that she was “terrified” when the quake struck. “The office swayed violently side to side. I was afraid it would collapse. Everyone panicked,” Hara said. The quake’s epicentre was about 12 miles (20km) south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city, with a population of about 700,000. The US Geological Survey initially said the earthquake had a magnitude of 7.1, but revised it later to 6.8. The tremor at 4.27 pm local time had a magnitude of 7.1, the JMA said, but reached the highest level of 7 on Japan’s shindo scale. A subsequent aftershock with a magnitude of 6.1 was registered at 5.08pm. Japan, which is located along the “ring of fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches in the Pacific basin, is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes. The country accounts for about 20% of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6 or more. The massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739. It damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a popular tourist site. Some of the castle’s stone walls were damaged in the most recent quake. Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had lost power, while the railway company JR Kyushu suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains. Kumamoto airport also shut its runway as airlines diverted and cancelled flights. The telecoms operators KDDI and NTT Docomo ‌said there was disruption to their mobile phone services owing to power shortages and transmission-line failures. There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan’s nuclear regulation authority said. The Japanese military has mobilised 3,600 personnel for disaster relief operations and sent 20 aircraft to assess the damage from the air, the defence minister said. Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that left around 18,500 people dead or missing and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.

title: US diplomats stage UN walkout after France criticizes human rights record under Trump
summary: France had also intervened after Trump administration had opposed the reappointment of UN human rights chief
body: US diplomats walked out of a United Nations meeting after France criticized the country’s human rights record under Donald Trump. The staged walkout, which occurred on Monday during a UN security council meeting on the Ukraine-Russia war, came days after the Trump administration cited “forced labor” allegations as it imposed sweeping tariffs on dozens of countries. Critics accused the US president of leaning on the claims as a “convenient” justification for the new duties, which were unveiled on Thursday. The following day, the Trump administration criticized the credibility of the UN human rights system and opposed the reappointment of Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, prompting an extraordinary intervention on social media from France’s UN mission in Geneva. “The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore,” the French Geneva mission said in response. “Today, it stands alongside North Korea, Nicaragua, Mali & Russia, isolated. And the world no longer listens to it. “#AmericaAlone,” it added. Last March, Türk said he was “deeply worried by the fundamental shift in direction” in the US. In June, Türk took sharp aim at the Trump administration by calling for “prompt, independent, impartial and effective investigations” into the deaths occurring in US government immigration custody. In addition to the US, nine other countries voted no to Türk’s re-appointment, including Russia, North Korea, Israel, Nicaragua and Mali. His re-appointment was ultimately approved, with 144 countries including France, China and the UK in favor, while 13 countries abstained. In response to the French mission’s post, the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, wrote on X on Sunday and said: “It is disappointing – though not surprising – that this is how France deflects on its shameful vote to coddle some of the worst human rights abusers. “France voted for someone who has been lecturing, free, sovereign democracies like the United States, the UK, and Israel, while cozying up to the world’s worst oppressors.” The US continued to criticize France during Monday’s meeting, with Dan Negrea, the US deputy ambassador, claiming that the US “remains the beacon of liberty for the world”. “As such, we will not be affording them the benefit of listening to their politicized drivel until they renounce their condescending and disrespectful rhetoric and behave in a manner commensurate with their seat on this council,” said Negrea. France’s UN ambassador, Jérôme Bonnafont, did not mention the walkout, instead saying on Monday: “The United Nations was created with the goal of working towards international peace and security, human rights and development,” the Associated Press reports. “All of that forms the spirit in which France works within the United Nations … to preserve this institution, its independence, its ability to act in service of the charter and act to serve human rights and peace.” The US walkout came after Trump faced bipartisan criticism over his use of “forced labor” as “a pretext” for imposing controversial new tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on imports from more than 80 countries. Those include longstanding allies such as the UK, Canada, Australia, and the European Union, alongside Mexico, India and China. Criticizing the tariffs, Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the House’s ways and means committee, said last week: “Forced labor is a real and pervasive problem in our supply chains and demands serious enforcement. It should never be cheapened into a pretext for a tariff policy built on dubious legal theories and personal grievances.’’

title: Seattle police recover machine gun and ghost gun from scene of mass shooting
summary: Three people died, including one of the suspects, and at least five more were wounded, including two-year-old boy
body: Seattle police recovered a modified machine gun and an untraceable “ghost gun” from the scene of a mass shooting at a food festival this weekend that left three people dead – including one of the suspects – and at least five more wounded, the police chief, Shon Barnes, said on Tuesday. Sunday’s shooting appeared to involve at least three suspects, Barnes said at a televised news conference. One of those three, 19-year-old Junior Cee Niko Semo, died at the scene. A second, 15-year-old suspect was disarmed and arrested at the scene. At least one more suspect remains at large, Barnes said. The shooting broke out in the middle of a three-day food festival at Seattle Center, a park located near the city’s Space Needle. Two people whom Seattle police say were uninvolved in the shooting were killed: Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and Ashley Whitehead, 56. People wounded by crossfire included a two-year-old boy. Others were trampled as the crowd rushed to safety. Casings from fired cartridges and three pistols were recovered from the scene, police say. Police seized a 9mm ghost gun produced from a parts kit made by the now-defunct company Polymer80 from the 15-year-old suspect at the scene. They also recovered a Glock pistol modified with an auto sear, or “switch”, allowing it to be fired as a fully automatic machine gun. Both of those pistols had extended magazines, with the Glock holding 40 rounds and the ghost gun holding 33. The state of Washington generally bans firearms from carrying more than 10 rounds. Both types of weapon have raised concerns among law enforcement officials in recent years, for different reasons. Illegal machine guns increase a firearm’s rate of fire while reducing the shooter’s accuracy. Ghost guns make it easier for prohibited persons to acquire firearms and harder for law enforcement officials to trace weapons used in crimes. The third gun, a .45-caliber pistol, was not used in the crime. Police did not so far believe that any of the recovered firearms had been stolen, though authorities were still working on tracing the two serialized guns. Cheap, user-installed auto sears or switches that allow shooters to convert semiautomatic pistols into fully automatic machine guns have proliferated in the age of 3D printing and internet shopping. Unserialized “ghost guns” were legal to buy and assemble under federal law from parts kit manufacturers like Polymer80, until the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives started regulating them as firearms in 2022. The advent of 3D printing, however, has made it easier for private individuals to produce ghost guns illegally. Police were still trying to locate a person who showed up at a nearby hospital with what may have been a gunshot wound, but had not been confirmed as a victim of Sunday’s shooting, Barnes said. Authorities are continuing to review physical evidence, digital recordings and camera footage from the shooting scene to reconstruct what happened and locate at least one suspect who remains at large. There may be more than one at-large suspect involved in the shooting, Barnes said. The shooting was probably linked to gang violence, according to Seattle police. “We’re working to determine the groups involved and what their relationship may be,” Barnes said.

title: Former Gavin Newsom aide shares fresh details of affair
summary: Ruby Rippey writes in Vanity Fair of relationship with then San Francisco mayor and appears to contradict his account
body: A former aide to Gavin Newsom has publicly shared for the first time her full account of their affair, which took place more than two decades ago when Newsom was mayor of San Francisco. In a new essay published in Vanity Fair on Tuesday, Ruby Rippey writes about her struggles with alcoholism, substance abuse and her relationship with Newsom while she worked as his appointments secretary and was married to his deputy chief of staff and later the manager of the mayor’s re-election campaign. The essay provides the most detailed look yet at Rippey’s relationship with Newsom, now in the final year of his second term as governor of California – and is likely to rekindle interest in the scandal ahead of his widely expected run for the White House in 2028. In the essay, Rippey does not refer to Newsom by name, but as her “boss” and the “mayor”. “For my former boss, it is a footnote in a longer arc of ascent,” Rippey writes in the Vanity Fair essay, titled How I Blew Up – Then Rebuilt – My Life. “For me, it is the fracture that split my life into before and after.” Newsom, who was single at the time, publicly admitted to the relationship in 2007, memorably telling reporters at a city hall press conference: “Everything you’ve heard and read is true.” In his new memoir, Newsom describes their relationship as “the briefest of affairs”. But Rippey’s telling complicates his account of their story. Newsom writes in his new book that he “came clean” to her husband and his top aide Alex Tourk – a version Rippey says gives Newsom “credit for something I had already done”. “Technically defensible, perhaps, but one that leaves the unmistakable impression that he, not I, was the one who told Alex the truth,” she writes. In the essay, Rippey describes the early days of the newly elected mayor’s administration, her marriage, pregnancy, struggles with alcohol and her ensuing relationship with Newsom as it veered into an extramarital affair. She eventually went to rehab and left her job with the mayor’s office. After the story became public, Rippey was inundated with calls from journalists and was the subject of frenzied media coverage about the affair. Jennifer Siebel Newsom, the first partner of California who started dating Newsom shortly afterward, told journalists in 2007 that Rippey was the “culprit”– remarks she later apologized for. The office of the governor and a spokesperson for Siebel Newsom did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the aftermath of the incident, Kamala Harris, then the district attorney, contacted Rippey, she writes. Rippey was being urged to speak publicly about the incident, she told Harris, who advised her to pause and that taking time would give her “better perspective”. “It turns out to be the best advice I receive. I am newly sober and still inside the wreckage – unable to make sense of anything, let alone speak clearly about it,” Rippey writes. Rippey and her husband eventually divorced. For years, Rippey said little publicly about her relationship with Newsom. During the MeToo movement, she observed a new narrative about their relationship emerge in which Rippey saw herself cast as a “powerless subordinate”, she writes. At the time, Rippey said she was doubtful it applied to her situation. Although she was Newsom’s “subordinate”, she said in 2018, she was also “a free-thinking, 33-year-old, adult married woman and mother. Also happened to have an unfortunate inclination toward drinking-to-excess and self-destruction.” Taking responsibility felt like the last form of agency, Rippey writes in the essay. But since the reckoning, she has re-evaluated the role power can play in a relationship between a subordinate and their boss. “Both things are true,” she writes. “I am responsible for what I did. Power does not distribute consequences evenly.” Rippey is now 20 years sober, she writes, and has remarried and rebuilt her relationship with her ex-husband.

title: New York offers college admission for residents unenrolled from Howard University
summary: Historically Black institution withdrew more than 500 first-year students for missed tuition payments
body: New York residents who were unenrolled from Washington DC’s Howard University have been offered a reprieve after the historically Black institution withdrew more than 500 first-year students for missed tuition payments in late July. On 27 July, Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, announced that affected New Yorkers can seek admission at the City University of New York (Cuny) and the State University of New York (Suny) for the fall 2026 semester. Students will be offered expedited late admissions review at the Suny campuses at Buffalo, Albany, Buffalo State University, Binghamton, Oneonta, Stony Brook and New Paltz, with other schools assessing capacity. “Hundreds of students, including New Yorkers, are scrambling and scared since they’ve been disenrolled from their intended college just a few weeks before classes are set to begin,” Hochul said in a statement. “New York is home to the nation’s finest systems of public higher education, and we are ready to welcome these talented students with the opportunity they deserve. To every student who is worried that their educational future has been disrupted: New York is ready to support and empower you.” Howard University said that 502 students did not submit their tuition payments by the school’s 10 July deadline, despite notifications that began in March. But some students have shared on social media that they never received the notifications. “I worked like crazy to get into this school,” Saniah Collins told the AP. The school sent her an email last week notifying her that she had missed the payment deadline. “Howard has been my everything. My whole senior year, my whole summer I worked consistently on scholarships. We tried to make ourselves 10 steps ahead to make sure we were on the right page.” The disenrollment follows a similar predicament last year where hundreds of students were unable to register for Howard University’s fall 2025 classes due to long-overdue balances. Most of the accounts were resolved in the following months; in early September 2025, Howard University told the Guardian that only 150 students had not registered for fall 2025 classes. At the time, Howard had transitioned from its BisonWeb platform to the new BisonHub platform, which caused a delay in about 1,000 student account updates between January and June 2025. “Past due student balances are not the result of delayed account updates. The past due balances occurred when students did not resolve their balances by the specified date,” Howard University said in a statement to the Guardian in September 2025. “Each student’s financial situation is unique, and we recognize that many of our students are doing everything they can to remain in good financial standing. Because of the system changeover, the university understands that there may have been some legitimate misunderstanding of amounts due to resolve long overdue balances. However, each long overdue balance should have been well understood and resolved by the student.” Last year, students created a movement called “Whose Howard Is It” to demand better financial aid support.

title: Lindsey Graham remembered as ‘true American original’ at Capitol memorial
summary: ‘He died doing the work he was born to do,’ Trump says as political leaders honor Republican US senator
body: Donald Trump and other political leaders convened in Washington for the memorial of the long-serving US senator Lindsey Graham on Tuesday afternoon, remembering the “swashbuckling” South Carolina Republican “a true American original” whose embrace of “America First” never softened his advocacy for a staunch interventionist US foreign policy. Graham, a polarizing figure and onetime rival turned stalwart ally of Trump, was known for championing the US-Israel war on Iran and was a prominent voice in the anti-abortion movement and a unwavering supporter of Israel, serving as one of Capitol Hill’s most outspoken foreign policy hawks. “He died doing the work he was born to do, he was truly a great politician, serving the country he loved to serve so deeply,” Trump said of Graham in his eulogy at the National Cathedral. “He went out at the peak of his career, the top of his game as a legend that every one of us, many of us here today, blessed to know him and a friend that none of us will ever forget,” he added. Trump took the opportunity to reiterate his support for Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to the late senator’s seat for the remainder of his term. And he focused on Graham’s foreign policy record as a war hawk. “I will tell you, he never saw a war that he didn’t like. Only his true friends would understand that. But he wanted it for the good of our country,” he said. The president, who ran against Graham in the 2016 presidential election, admitted that “Lindsey and I did not exactly get off to the best of starts.” Recalling his leaking of Graham’s phone number to the public after Graham called him a “jackass” during the presidential race, Trump said: “It was Lindsey who had the last laugh because while I blew up his phone all for one day, we became great friends, and Lindsey did not stop calling me for the next 10 years. It was not easy.” Other speakers included the Fox News host Sean Hannity, who said Graham would have been honored by the presence of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who held meetings with Trump earlier in the day. The television host also turned to flattery with Trump in the pews. “Lindsey, Mr President, I would argue in my mind probably has a heavenly version of Mar-a-Lago. It may even be a little bigger … Because he would want to obviously duplicate his dearest friend in life. You, Mr President,” he said. Speaking during a ceremony earlier on Tuesday inside the Capitol Rotunda, the US Senate majority leader, John Thune, hailed Graham as a “fierce defender of Ukraine”, following its full-scale invasion by Russia in 2022, and a “powerful voice for the [anti-abortion] movement”. “I feel his absence every day, and I know my colleagues do as well,” Thune, growing emotional, continued. “I look forward to the days when you make us laugh again.” Darline Graham, who was sworn in earlier this month, attended both services. She is running in the Republican primary to permanently succeed him. Graham died suddenly earlier this month, aged 71, shortly after returning to Washington from a trip to Kyiv. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, are due to attend an afternoon service for Graham at Washington National Cathedral. JD Vance, the US vice-president, credited Graham with the successful confirmation of Brett Kavanaugh to the US supreme court in 2018, which helped conservatives secure a supermajority on the bench within two years. “I believe that he saved that nomination,” Vance said. “I choose to remember Lindsey Graham as a person who could fight with you on one issue, but fight for you on another issue,” Vance said. “I remember Lindsey Graham as a man who loved people, and because he loved people, he was willing to reason with them, to respect them and ultimately to persuade them.” “May God rest the soul of Senator Lindsey Graham, a true American original,” he said. A former air force lawyer who served in the air force reserve while in Congress, Graham was elected to the House of Representatives in 1994 and served as a manager during Bill Clinton’s 1999 impeachment trial before winning a Senate seat in 2002. Weeks before his death, Graham defeated a field of challengers to win the Republican nomination in his bid for a fifth term. On Wednesday, in Graham’s home state, ceremonies will begin with services and an F-16 flyover at the South Carolina state house in Columbia, followed by a procession to First Baptist church for a public service. A private family burial will take place in Pickens county, home to Central, the small town where Graham and his younger sister and Senate successor, Darline, were born.

title: Utah woman set fire to church a day before wedding, authorities say
summary: Lenita Moreno, 25, arrested over fire – which allegedly caused $108,000 in damage – at Mormon church in Kaysville
body: A Utah woman set fire to the church where she was scheduled to get married a day before the wedding, allege authorities investigating what may have been an extreme case of cold feet. Lenita Moreno, 25, was arrested on a count of aggravated arson in connection with the 10 July blaze, which investigators say caused $108,000 in damage and was started using a tampon and other flammable items. According to court documents reported on by Utah news outlet KUTV, the fire started in the Relief Society room of a Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints building when Moreno, her unidentified groom and family members were setting up in the church building for the couple’s wedding the next day. The family reportedly said they were about to leave the church in Kaysville when the fire alarm went off. A bystander used water from wedding decorations to put out the blaze while another used a fire extinguisher, said the documents cited by KUTV. Investigators said the fire appeared to have been started under a chair using “items that were out of the ordinary, including what appeared to be a tampon”. The groom allegedly told detectives he and Moreno were in the room where the fire started. He also reportedly told detectives he and Moreno had been to an Ace Hardware earlier in the day. Police said they contacted the store, and employees there provided video footage of Moreno stealing two cigarette lighters. Police alleged they could see Moreno walk towards the lighters, take an unknown number and hide them on her person. They said Moreno admitted to stealing from the Ace Hardware, but that she would not disclose what she had taken. “It is believed that Lenita (Tessa) started a fire within a church building while five others were still inside,” the probable cause stated. “Lenita did not obtain a marriage license for her own wedding that was to occur the following day after the fire but had lied stating she had.” Beside arson, Moreno was booked with retail theft and providing false information to a peace officer. Moreno, who KUTV reported was set to be married under the name of Tessa Moran, was being held without bail as of Tuesday. The US event insurance company Eventsure estimates that 15 to 20% of weddings are called off. While a change of heart is not covered under a policy, Eventsured states: “Sometimes you have to cancel your wedding for reasons out of your control whether it’s a fire, illness, etc. “In these cases, consider getting cancellation insurance.”

title: Paco Robles obituary
summary: Other lives: Refugee from Spanish civil war who settled in the UK but maintained connections with his homeland
body: My family friend Paco (Francisco) Robles, who has died aged 99, was one of the last survivors of the largest ever single day’s migration into the UK, when on 23 May 1937 about 4,000 people arrived in Southampton fleeing the Spanish civil war. Paco, who was 10 at the time, and his younger sister, Maria Jesus, were among 3,800 children on board the ageing former cruise ship the Habana, along with volunteer teachers, priests and supporters. Two aunts of mine, Poppy and Chloe Vulliamy, had become involved in helping to get the children out of the country, and Chloe ran the first two hostels that Paco stayed in, as well as the last to close, in 1951. In 2017 Paco unveiled a blue plaque at the first house, in Wherstead Park in Suffolk, near Ipswich, and spoke emotionally of Chloe’s role as his surrogate mother. He was delighted to discover that the tree he had climbed there remained intact, 80 years later. Paco was born in León, in north western Spain, to Martina (nee Hernando), a maid, and Germillano, a deputy for the Socialist party in the city. When Paco was young the family moved to the Basque Country, where his father worked in the chemical department of a steelworks in Bilbao. After the nearby town of Guernica was heavily bombed by German and Italian planes in support of General Franco’s nationalist forces in April 1937, his parents managed to get him and his sister on board the Habana. Life on arrival was not easy; the UK government refused to provide any public funding for the care of the children, and so Paco was educated at volunteer-run residential homes known as a “colonies” – where he encountered my aunt Chloe. Once Franco had attained victory over the republicans in the civil war, he demanded the return of the niños who had left – but that often proved impossible. In Paco’s case, as in many others, there was nothing to go back to: his father had been imprisoned, the family home had been stolen, and his mother was struggling to survive, with little food to eat. He therefore remained in Britain, and worked over the years in various jobs, including at a munitions factory, a bakery and as a labourer on a farm. Like many of his fellow Habana refugees he felt neither Spanish in Spain nor British in the UK. But his experiences left him skilled in connecting and communicating with people, and throughout his life he maintained his Spanish connections, including as a strong supporter of the Basque Childrens’ Association and as a regular visitor to a Spanish social centre in London, where he lived. Paco married Maria Román, a factory worker, in 1949; she died in 2012. He is survived by their three children, Elena, Fernando and Maria, six grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren.

title: Trump reportedly pushing RFK Jr to cut vaccines more aggressively
summary: White House has halted changing vaccine schedule as it is unpopular, but anti-vaxx Trump set on ‘alleviating autism’
body: Donald Trump is pushing the longtime vaccine opponent and current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr to be more aggressive on cutting vaccines in the US, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal. Trump has a long record of anti-vaccine statements, but the White House recently put a hold on vaccine changes after polling indicated they were a losing issue in the midterm elections. Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services, recently slashed the routine childhood immunization schedule in an unprecedented move. Trump reportedly asked Kennedy at his northern Virginia golf course in May if the health secretary had the “yips”, according to the Journal. Trump wasn’t talking about a sudden inability to make putts. Kennedy wasn’t making enough cuts to the US vaccination schedule, Trump reportedly said. The US president hopes to make “alleviating autism” a component of his legacy, the Journal reported – and he has taken issue with Kennedy’s less aggressive changes to vaccination recommendations in recent months. “Donald Trump has been anti-vaccine at least since 2015,” said Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center and an infectious diseases physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. At the Republican primary debate that year, Trump said that autism had gotten “totally out of control” and vaccines should be in “smaller doses over a longer period of time”. Trump regularly posted on social media about debunked links between vaccination and autism as early as 2014, and his posts on Truth Social have recently advocated for breaking up shots into individual components and delaying some childhood vaccines for more than a decade. Tony Fabrizio, a top pollster for Trump, found that anti-vaccine moves are unpopular with voters in key districts, concluding in a December memo that “skepticism toward vaccine requirements is politically risky for both parties”. Susie Wiles gave HHS the deadline of New Year’s Eve to make vaccine changes, to allow vaccines to fall into the background with the midterms looming, according to reporting by the Rolling Stone. But Trump’s priorities appear to lie elsewhere. He issued a memo, two days after Fabrizio’s poll results, directing HHS to align with “peer” nations on vaccination recommendations, even though the US was already making similar recommendations to other countries. A month later, Kennedy slashed vaccine recommendations by one-third, from 17 to 11. A federal judge ordered a halt to these changes following a lawsuit in March from the American Academy of Pediatrics. The judge also paused the work of the advisory committee on immunization practices (ACIP), which was illegally formed under Kennedy, he said. Kennedy has not made any significant changes to the vaccine schedule since then, though he has continued speaking about autism and its potential causes, and the US government is appealing the judge’s stay on vaccine changes. Kennedy also sought to divert $5bn in funding – more than 10% of the entire National Institutes of Health budget – toward research on vaccines and autism, according to reporting by Reuters. Decades of research into the causes of autism point overwhelmingly to genetics, and dozens of studies have indicated no link between vaccines and autism. Even so, Trump issued an executive order in May urging HHS to change vaccine recommendations. Kush Desai, a spokesperson for the White House, did not dispute the details reported by the Journal and others in a statement to the Guardian. He instead pointed to parents of autistic children – but not to autistic people themselves – with “questions and concerns” who “have long been ignored if not mocked”. The Trump administration was “committed to leaving no stone unturned” to address those concerns, Desai added. Kennedy and Trump are “aligned in their commitment” to confront the “chronic disease epidemic affecting America’s children”, said Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, in an apparent reference to autism. HHS would “continue to pursue evidence-based research to identify the root causes of autism and other chronic diseases”, she added. “I think Donald Trump has a fixed, immutable belief that vaccines cause autism,” Offit said. That makes Trump the most powerful anti-vaxxer in the world, Offit said – and it means he is unlikely to fire Kennedy, even as rumors have swirled that the health secretary is on his way out. The abrupt rise of measles and other deadly diseases are more likely to be Trump’s legacy than advances in understanding autism, Offit said. As top leaders have downplayed the safety and importance of vaccines, measles has surged to its highest rate in 30 years, and the nation has suffered a rise in deaths from whooping cough, flu and tetanus in recent years. “And our commander in chief, our vaccine guy in chief, is our president. He’s fine with this. Just as RFK Jr is fine with this,” Offit said. “Trump has become the president of Measles Land,” Offit added. “That should bother him.”

title: Zelenskyy and Netanyahu brave the whims of Trump’s darkly confounding White House
summary: Ukrainian and Israeli leaders converge on Washington with criss-crossing fortunes, but knowing they can count on little from US counterpart
body: The converging visits of Benjamin Netanyahu and Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Washington offer an unusually eloquent snapshot of a world in turmoil, unmoored from decades-old certainties. Some things remain the same. The US is still an almighty military and economic power and for both foreign visitors, a White House encounter with Donald Trump is critical to their governments and the wars they are fighting. The imperial presidency Trump has tried to forge is in decline, however, in large part as a result of his own erratic leadership. He may see his visitors as client-potentates flying in from the edges of empire to kiss his ring. But they will be as aware of Trump’s weaknesses as they are of their own. Netanyahu and Zelenskyy arrive in Washington on opposite trajectories. The Israeli prime minister’s star has declined dramatically since he persuaded Trump to join him in an ill-conceived war on Iran five months ago, on the groundless promise that the Tehran regime would quickly collapse. Since then, a viscerally disappointed president has publicly scolded Netanyahu and insisted Netanyahu would ultimately do his bidding, while the White House has liberally leaked Trump’s foul-mouthed tirades belittling him. Israel has been left out of negotiations with Iran, and its views were ignored when it came to selling F-35 stealth fighter planes to Turkey, or making a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia. An Economist/YouGov survey found that nearly half of Americans polled thought that Netanyahu should be arrested on arrival for war crimes. By contrast, Zelenskyy arrived in Washington in the ascendant. Ukraine has defied the US administration’s predictions of inevitable defeat to Russia’s might, his country is now a world leader in drone warfare, and parts of the Magaverse are now warming to the accidental war leader they once scorned as a loser. In traditional administrations, both men and the countries they represent would be natural allies and both could be sure of solid welcome in the Oval Office. It is telling that the occasion of their coinciding visits was the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican hawk of the old school who could be relied on for wholehearted promotion of the Israeli and Ukrainian war efforts. In that respect, he was one of a dying breed. But this is no normal administration, led by a president who rules on a whim, and neither visitor can predict how he will be received. Neither wanted cameras in the room. Trump began his presidency by throwing all-in support behind Netanyahu and his wars, dropping even the pretence of concern for the lives of Palestinians or the people of southern Lebanon that had tempered backing for Israel from earlier presidents. Facing a hostile electorate, the president is trying to extricate himself from the region, but in doing so is finding Israel the most recalcitrant party on every front. In Ukraine, Trump threw out the American foreign policy handbook altogether, proposing peace deals that often echoed Moscow’s talking points, rewarding aggression with territory Russia had not even won on the battlefield. Rather than capitulate, Ukraine showed it could fight on despite drastic cuts in US military aid, relying more on Europe and its own hard-won improvised expertise. Now Zelenskyy finds himself the unlikely darling of far-right Maga influencers such as Lara Loomer, formerly an apologist for the Russian invasion, who interviewed the Ukrainian president in his garden last week, and called for “moral clarity” in Kyiv’s support. Zelenskyy’s recent ascent may mirror Netanyahu’s simultaneous decline, but that does not mean they came to Washington with comparable status. When it comes to the Trump administration, they arrive from very different starting positions. Just about anything would count as an upgrade for Zelenskyy compared with his infamous White House ambush in February 2025 by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, who tried to humiliate the Ukrainian visitor in front of the cameras, demanding gratitude and acceptance of defeat with “no cards” left to play. Zelenskyy does have cards this time but well short of a winning hand without US support. The Ukrainian’s immediate aim is modest: for Trump to honour Senator Graham by backing a Russia sanctions bill he was pushing at the time of his death. He knows that direct US military aid to Ukraine is not likely to return in meaningful quantities any time soon. The Patriot interceptors and other weapons Ukraine once counted on for its defence have been used up wholesale in the Middle East, many of them to protect Israel. It will take years for the US to rebuild its own stocks. Netanyahu may be out of favour in the current White House, but the US is committed to Israel’s defence in a manner and on a scale of which Ukraine can only dream. Netanyahu and Zelenskyy came to Washington on different paths and footings but they do at least share an awareness that their relationship with the administration can be upended with scant notice, without any clear reasons, in a matter of mere seconds in the court of the irascible, flagging would-be emperor.

title: Deaths feared after ‘many people’ trapped inside Japanese shopping centre following earthquake – as it happened
body: The Kumamoto region located in the southwestern island of Kyushu was the epicentre of the earthquake and it is no stranger to such disasters. In 2016, the volcanic area was the hardest hit by a series of earthquakes, the highest was a 7.0-magnitude just beneath Kumamoto city. In total 277 people were killed, either directly by the earthquake or due to disaster related injuries At the time, the Guardian reported that tens of thousands of people were evacuated from Mashiki, one of the the worst hit towns. The Kumamoto Prefecture lies at the southern end of the Japan Median Tectonic Line, Japan’s longest tectonic zone. Hundreds of injured people have been transported to medical facilities throughout Kumamoto Prefecture, but some hospitals have had to cease operations due to power outages and other issues. According to a report compiled by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, as of 10pm local time, 43 medical institutions in Kumamoto Prefecture have suffered damage such as power outages, water shortages, and inability to use medical gas. According to the Kyushu Electric Power Transmission and Distribution website, as of 01:30am local time, over 40,000 households in Kumamoto Prefecture are experiencing power outages. Four people have been rescued from the scene at the Aeon shopping mall, and none of them are in life-threatening condition. The whereabouts of 10 people still remains unknown. A senior government official told reporters: “We don’t know if it was the cause of the explosion, but there have been reports that gas was leaking. The main gas valve has been shut off, and the police, fire department, and Self-Defense Forces are conducting rescue operations.” Footage captured inside a Costco in Kumamoto shows shoppers ducking for cover after shelves collapse as the earthquake hit. Japan’s public broadcaster NHK are reporting that two people are in cardiac arrest and nine others are missing following a chimney collapse at Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro plant in the Kumamoto. According to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, local firefighters reported that “there are nine people who need to be rescued”. According to Kumamoto Prefecture, two people were found in a state of cardiopulmonary arrest. The Aeon mall had just reopened last month as as a new and improved shopping and entertainment complex to commemorate its recovery from the magnitude 7.3 Kumamoto earthquake of 2016, which had left it badly damaged and in need of rebuilding, according to Reuters. A 6.8-magnitude earthquake has shaken south Japan, leaving at least 50 people injured. Some are trapped and presumed dead inside a shopping mall. The earthquake hit the Kumamoto prefecture on the southern Kyushu island late on Tuesday afternoon, knocking out power to thousands of homes and damaging roads, bridges and buildings. Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, told reporters authorities were still assessing the extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by another deadly quake a decade ago. “We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages ⁠and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” Takaichi said. “I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.” An explosion occurred in an Aeon shopping mall shortly after the earthquake, trapping “many people”, fire services said. The broadcaster TBS reported that police said “quite a few” were presumed dead. About 20 to 30 workers at the mall were unaccounted for, NHK said. An Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated after the initial quake and the cause of the explosion remained unclear. Footage showed one side of the mall, the prefecture’s largest with roughly 200 stores, was torn away, exposing steel beams ‌and strewing debris across the neighbouring car park. Several ambulances and fire engines were parked outside as rescue teams searched for survivors. About 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, ⁠the disaster management agency said. The areas with the biggest tremors will remain at risk of further strong quakes and landslides for about a week since the shallow earthquake is triggering active seismic activity in the area, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. So far there have been more than 60 aftershocks ranging in magnitude from 1 to 4, the agency said. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after the quake, but was lifted within two hours. One person was killed in south-west Japan when a house collapsed during the earthquake, Kyodo News reported. One hospital reported more than 50 injuries, and another about 40, including 10 in a serious condition, the public broadcaster NHK said. Several people on a high-speed ‌train at the time of the quake were also ‌injured and multiple people were unaccounted for after a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, according to local media reports. The quake’s epicentre was about 12 miles (20km) south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city, with a population of about 700,000. The US Geological Survey initially said the earthquake had a magnitude of 7.1, but revised it later to 6.8. Read our full report here: A gas leak may have caused the explosion at the shopping mall where it is feared that a “considerable number” of people may have died. A senior government official told Japanese reporters that Aeon Mall Kumamoto had reported a gas leak, according to NHK. The official told journalists that whilst the cause of the explosion has not yet been verified, the main gas valve has now been shut off, and police, fire departments, and the Self-Defense Forces are conducting rescue operations. An Aeon spokesperson said earlier in the day that the cause of the explosion remained unclear. When the explosion occurred at southern Kumamoto’s largest shopping mall, a dashcam in a car driving near the scene captured the moment of the explosion. A shopping centre has partially collapsed in a 6.8 magnitude earthquake in south-western Japan leaving people trapped inside, according to emergency services. Today’s earthquake registered a 7.1 magnitude, although that was later revised down to 6.8 by the US Geological Survey. This graphic shows the shake intensity spreading out from the epicentre of the quake. Here are are some of the latest photos of damage caused by the earthquake… It is feared that a “considerable number” of people have died in a shopping mall damaged by a major earthquake in southwestern Japan, broadcaster TBS said. TV Asahi also reported that there had been “several deaths” at the shopping mall, citing a local police source. Meanwhile, Fuji TV also reported there had been fatalities. Emergency services earlier said “many people” were trapped inside the building after a floor collapsed. Around 20 to 30 workers at southern Kumamoto’s largest shopping mall were unaccounted for after it was rocked by an explosion in the ‌aftermath of the quake, NHK said. Fire services earlier said ‌multiple people were trapped inside. One side of the mall, which houses around 200 stores, was torn away, exposing steel beams ‌and strewing debris across a vast parking lot, footage showed. Several ambulances and fire engines were parked outside, as rescue teams searched for survivors. A spokesperson for mall operator Aeon said customers and employees were evacuated right after the initial quake and that the exact cause of the ensuing explosion was unclear. The US Geological Survey initially said the earthquake had a magnitude of 7.1, but subsequently revised it down to 6.8. “Several” people are missing from the Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro plant in the Kumamoto prefecture after a chimney collapsed there, according to a report by Japan’s public broadcaster, NHK, which cited the Yatsushiro police station as its source of information. The report added that police and firefighters are investigating the matter. The plant is located in Yatsushiro City. As we mentioned in an earlier post, Kumamoto Castle, one of Japan’s oldest and most renowned castles, was damaged after today’s powerful earthquake hit. In a brief social media post, the castle’s management wrote: Due to the impact of the Kumamoto regional earthquake that occurred earlier, today’s operations will be suspended. We ask everyone to prioritize your own safety above all else in your actions. There have been more than 60 aftershocks ranging in magnitude from 1 to 4, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. Kyodo News agency said a hospital in Yatsushiro city accepted about 40 people with injuries from the quake. A train was derailed and fell on its side at the Yatsushiro station, and stone walls were damaged at the Kumamoto castle, Kyodo said. Yozo Kai, a priest at a Shinto shrine in the nearby town of Mashiki, said a few stone lanterns fell down. “I worried if the main hall and the gate would tilt again,” he told Kyodo. “The shaking reminded me of the Kumamoto quake (10 years ago) and I was frightened,” said Hiroki Shimoda, an official at the Mifune town hall, who saw rooftiles of nearby homes crash down to the ground. Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had lost power as a result of the latest quake, while railway company JR Kyushu said that it had suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains. Kumamoto airport also shut its runway, as airlines diverted and cancelled flights. Telecoms operators KDDI and Docomo said there was disruption to their mobile ‌phone services due to power shortages and transmission-line failures. There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan’s nuclear regulation authority said. Around 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said. The quake’s epicentre was about 20 kilometres south of Kumamot…

title: Trump hosts back-to-back meetings with Zelenskyy and Netanyahu
summary: Ukraine seeks more firepower for air defenses and Israeli prime minister tries to repair relationship with US president
body: Donald Trump hosted back-to-back White House meetings with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday, as Ukraine seeks more firepower for its air defenses and the Israeli prime minister tries to repair his strained relationship with the US president. It was Netanyahu’s first visit to the Oval Office since he and Trump launched their joint military campaign against Iran on 28 February. Netanyahu’s relationship with Trump has been complicated in recent weeks by his push to keep fighting Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon, even as Trump pursued a diplomatic opening with Tehran. Tensions between the pair have risen as the war has drifted inconclusively, with Trump calling the Israeli premier “crazy” and declaring: “Without me, there would be no Israel.” The two men are each facing pressure at home, with Netanyahu in a tough re-election fight, and Trump under pressure to end an unpopular war that has pushed up prices before November’s midterms. Trump signaled some of that friction beforehand. Asked on Fox & Friends on Tuesday morning about reports that Netanyahu planned to brief him on intelligence about Iranian activity at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site Trump has threatened to bomb, he said he knew “exactly what’s going on at Pickaxe”, adding that Netanyahu raises it because “he wants me to stay involved”. Far outside the White House, behind the fences, protesters chanted: “Netanyahu, you’re a tyrant” and “Bibi, you’re not welcome here” on Tuesday. The closed-door meeting, which lasted about an hour, was expected to cover Iran, a framework deal the US and Israel signed with Lebanon, and a possible expansion of the Abraham accords, according to a White House official. Netanyahu also faces the task of reassuring Trump he will not obstruct US-led diplomacy in Gaza and Lebanon, as support for Israel among the US public has slipped, with a new AP-Norc poll showing a sharp decline amid accusations, denied by Israel, that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide. Zelenskyy’s meeting was described by both sides as positive. In a statement, Zelenskyy said he had discussed licensing arrangements to let Ukraine manufacture its own interceptors for Patriot missile systems. “We also spoke about diplomacy – it’s important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated,” said Zelenskyy. “Our teams will arrange the details of their further communication. I am grateful to the United States for its firm support.” He opened by offering condolences over the death of the US senator Lindsey Graham, calling the late foreign policy hawk “a true friend of Ukraine”. Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, said afterwards that both meetings had been “positive and productive!”

title: Joe Biden appears to discuss sensitive information on tape with ghostwriter
summary: In recordings made in 2016 and 2017 former president also appears to describe possessing classified information
body: Former US president Joe Biden appeared to discuss sensitive information and describe possessing classified documents in audio recordings released on Monday by the Oversight Project, a conservative activist group. The heavily redacted transcripts and recordings were made in 2016 and 2017, while Biden was working with a ghostwriter on his 2017 memoir, Promise Me, Dad: A Year of Hope, Hardship, and Purpose. No classified material was ever alleged to have appeared in the book. Biden, at times, seems to struggle to remember certain details or dates regarding events and topics in the transcripts and recordings, prompting the Oversight Project – as well as some conservative media outlets – to allege that he was “already demonstrating significant cognitive decline” in the years before he ran for president. In a recording dated October 2016, near the end of Biden’s second term as vice- president under former president Barack Obama, Biden can be heard discussing notes he says he kept from his time in office. “There was a lot of stuff going on at the same time in foreign policy,” Biden said. “You didn’t want to go into it, but I have extensive notes … over this period of time.” “Oh, that’s in – oh, you actually have those here,” the writer responds. To which Biden says, “yeah, now, there’s a lot of other notes too”, and goes on to say: “These – this is my – they didn’t even know I had this. “Some of this stuff, I’m not, you know, going to – um so I go back, you know what I mean?” Biden continues. “I have stuff on, you know, five – here we go, I mean, it’s like … I have stuff on all the way up to 5/19.” A representative for Biden did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on Tuesday about the recordings. But a spokesperson for Biden told CBS News: “President Biden’s conversations for a book a decade ago that discussed his late son are private, and were provided to the Department of Justice on the express condition they stay that way. “Reversing course and making them public is just the latest example of this Administration weaponizing the DoJ for political retribution,” they added. “It’s wrong, and while President Biden disagrees with today’s decision, he also respects the courts and the vital role an independent judiciary plays in a healthy democracy.” Classified materials were also found at President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club after he left office following his first term. In 2024, a federal judge dismissed the case, ruling that the special counsel who brought the prosecution had been improperly appointed. The tapes of Biden appear to align with the findings in former special counsel Robert Hur’s 2024 report on his handling of classified documents. That report concluded that Biden had “willfully” kept and shared classified information “after his vice presidency when he was a private citizen” including “classified documents about military and foreign policy in Afghanistan” and handwritten notes about national security and foreign policy “implicating sensitive intelligence sources and methods”. The report also stated that Biden, during his eight years as vice-president, “regularly wrote notes by hand in notebooks” and that some of those notes “related to classified subjects” and that “some of the notes are themselves classified”. It also said that Biden “shared information, including some classified information, from those notebooks with his ghostwriter”. Hur described Biden as a “sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory”, prompting a furious response from the then president and his officials, and claimed that Biden’s “memory was significantly limited, both during his recorded interviews with the ghostwriter in 2017, and in his interview with our office in 2023”. But Hur ultimately determined that no criminal charges were warranted, in part because he said it would be hard to convince a jury that “a former president well into his 80s” was guilty of a felony that “requires a mental state of willfulness”. The Oversight Project, a branch of the Heritage Foundation, sued for the tapes, which had been handed over to the justice department during its investigation into Biden’s handling of the records. House judiciary committee Republicans also sought the tapes. Biden had fought the release, but recently withdrew his legal challenge after a federal appeals court rejected his effort. In another recording dated 3 November 2016, Biden tells the writer: “And, and then – and then the next thing I have here is – this is classified. It’s all – it goes through the 17th.” The context of this clip is not clear. In a separate recording dated 16 February 2017, about a month after Biden left office, Biden tells the ghostwriter: “After that diary entry, the next one, between that and the 7th of July” was a “was a long meeting on the security council on – and part of it’s classified”. Later in that recording, Biden says: “So this was – I, early on, in ’09 – I just found all of the classified stuff downstairs. I wrote the President a handwritten 40-page memorandum arguing against deploying additional troops to Iraq – I mean, to Afghanistan – on the grounds that it wouldn’t matter, that the day we left would be like the day before we arrived.” In a statement on Monday, the Oversight Project said that since 2024, it and the Heritage Foundation “fought tooth and nail to bring these tapes to light”.

title: South Korean stock market at three-month low as AI sell-off intensifies
summary: Samsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competition
body: The sell-off in AI stocks has intensified, driving South Korea’s stock market down to its lowest level in three months. Investors continued to ditch chip stocks on Tuesday, amid rising concerns about the huge amount of borrowing among AI companies to fund their datacentre expansion plans. The South Korean semiconductor companies SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell by more than 10%, dragging the country’s Kospi share index down by 11.5% to its lowest point since mid-April. US chip stocks extended their recent losses when Wall Street opened on Tuesday, with Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital Corp and Seagate Technology all down by more than 4%. The Nasdaq 100 index of leading tech stocks fell by as much as 1.8% at one point, briefly taken into market correction territory with stocks more than 10% below their early June record high. They later rebounded to settle roughly flat on the day. Apple bucked the trend, rising to briefly become the second ever company to pass the $5tn (£3.76tn) valuation mark as investors losing confidence in AI stocks sought a safe haven. Analysts attributed the tech sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, after a report by The Information that China had begun mass production of homegrown deep ultraviolet (DUV) chip-making tools. “We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chip-making equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chip making and chip equipment leaders,” said Jing Jie Yu, an equity analyst at Morningstar, adding that the sell-off was “largely a kneejerk reaction and overdone”. On Monday, shares in the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT rose by 466% when it floated on the Shanghai stock exchange, underlining China’s drive to create its own AI supply chain. Investors may also be growing jittery about the “circular funding” at the heart of the AI industry, through which artificial intelligence firms finance one another. On Monday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia was in discussions with OpenAI about providing $250bn (£188bn) for a massive datacentre project in Ohio. Backing from Nvidia, which has an investment grade credit rating, could make it less expensive to raise funding for the project. News of the talks knocked Nvidia’s shares on Monday; they closed 5% lower, while the cost of insuring the chip company’s debt against default using a credit default swap (CDS) rose. “The market reaction to the Nvidia news was swift. Nvidia fell 5% and closed the session below the $200-per-share mark. More importantly, Nvidia’s five-year CDS spiked, suggesting that it may not yet be the right time to buy the dip,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote. Some analysts have suggested that Beijing, trying to win a tech war with the US, is providing US companies with cheap AI systems, undercutting attempts by Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft and Google to dominate the spread of AI tools.
